title: Metabolic and endocrine derangements
definition: Disturbances of glucose, lactate, acid-base balance, electrolytes and the adrenal and thyroid axes in a dog with babesiosis. The clinically important ones are hypoglycaemia (glucose below 3.3 mmol/L), hyperlactataemia (lactate above 2 mmol/L), and a mixed metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis [R1][R2][R3].
definition_note: Working definition confirmed, with changes. These are markers of severe disease, not one syndrome: they occur together in collapsed, severely anaemic dogs. The cortisol and thyroxine changes are an adaptive stress response and a non-thyroidal illness pattern, not adrenal or thyroid disease [R4][R5]. Hypoglycaemia is the only one with a direct, proven treatment.
key_points: Measure glucose in every admitted dog; it is essential in collapsed dogs, puppies under 6 months and dogs with severe anaemia, vomiting or icterus [R1].
About 1 in 5 admitted B. rossi dogs is hypoglycaemic, often severely, and many show only collapse, not seizures [R1][R2].
A collapsed or obtunded dog with a low glucose may look like cerebral babesiosis; treat the glucose first and reassess [R1][R2].
Lactate that does not fall by half within 8 to 16 hours, or stays above 4.4 mmol/L, predicts death better than one admission value [R6][R7].
High cortisol and low thyroxine mark severe disease and death; they are not a reason to give steroids or thyroid hormone [R4][R5].
Mixed acid-base disorders are the rule in severe B. rossi disease; bicarbonate has no tested role [R3][R2].

description.heading: What it is
description.text: A group of laboratory changes of severe babesiosis. Hypoglycaemia, hyperlactataemia, metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis, low potassium and sodium, high cortisol and low thyroxine all cluster in collapsed, severely anaemic dogs [R2][R3][R8]. In B. rossi, glucose and lactate are inversely related, and dogs that die often have low glucose and high lactate together [R8][R2].

description.heading: How common, and in which dogs
description.text: B. rossi, Onderstepoort: hypoglycaemia below 3.3 mmol/L in 9% of 250 dogs at presentation and 19.8% of admitted dogs; 16 had 2.2 mmol/L or less [R1][R9]. In 320 B. rossi dogs, 19.2% were hypoglycaemic, 24.9% hyperglycaemic and 55.5% of 209 had lactate above 2 mmol/L [R2]. Collapse was the strongest risk factor for hypoglycaemia; young age, severe anaemia, icterus and vomiting also raised the risk; toy breeds and pregnant bitches did not [R1]. B. canis: hypokalaemia in 16 of 40 dogs and hypochloraemia in 36 of 40 in early disease [R10].

description.heading: When in the course of disease
description.text: The changes are present at admission, before treatment [R1][R2]. In experimental B. rossi infection of 5 dogs, cortisol rose and thyroxine fell as parasitaemia rose, with peaks at 96 to 144 hours after infection, and both moved back towards baseline after diminazene treatment [R11]. Thyroid values in acutely ill dogs of other causes can stay abnormal for up to 21 days of recovery [R12].

description.heading: Mechanism
description.text: Hypoglycaemia is not caused by excess insulin: insulin was appropriately low in most hypoglycaemic B. rossi dogs [R13]. High glucose use by anaerobic glycolysis in severe anaemia, depleted liver glycogen and poor gluconeogenesis are suggested, not proven [R13][R9]. Lactate comes from tissue hypoxia. The acid-base picture mixes lactic and hyperchloraemic acidosis with hypoalbuminaemic alkalosis and respiratory alkalosis, so pH and bicarbonate alone mislead [R3][R14].

species_notes.note: Almost all glucose, lactate, cortisol and thyroid outcome data come from Onderstepoort B. rossi cohorts, which overlap; treat them as about three independent sources [R1][R2][R4][R6].

Electrolyte and acid-base series from Poland and Croatia: hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia, chloride changes in both directions, and mixed disorders in half of 14 dogs [R10][R15][R14]. In 15 Swiss dogs, all 8 non-survivors had hyperlactataemia (median 8.35 mmol/L) [R16]. Low T3, T4 and TSH were found in 13 dogs [R17].
In an Indian series, lactate was one of the markers that predicted death [R18]. No glucose or endocrine treatment data were found.

criteria.threshold: glucose below 3.3 mmol/L; severe at 2.2 mmol/L or less
criteria.note: Used in the B. rossi studies [R1][R2][R9].

criteria.threshold: glucose above 5.5 mmol/L (5.6 mmol/L in one study)
criteria.note: Common, never severe in 250 B. rossi dogs; not a reliable marker of severity [R2][R9].

criteria.threshold: lactate above 2 mmol/L (2.5 mmol/L in one study); above 5 mmol/L at admission is high risk
criteria.note: The original thresholds were published in other units; the mmol/L values are those of a South African review [R6][R7][R2].

criteria.threshold: above 2.5 mmol/L at 8, 16 or 24 h, or less than 50% fall within 8 to 16 h
criteria.note: Serial measurements in 90 dogs with severe or complicated babesiosis [R6][R7].

criteria.threshold: pCO2 more than 2 mmHg below that expected for the fall in bicarbonate
criteria.note: Expected fall: 0.7 mmHg pCO2 for each 1 mmol/L fall in bicarbonate; met in 76% of B. rossi dogs tested [R2].

clinical_signs.note: Most hypoglycaemic dogs present collapsed; only 2 of 23 had seizures [R1][R9].
Seen in 3 hypoglycaemic dogs and corrected at once with dextrose [R9][R7].
Hypoglycaemic surviving B. rossi dogs had a lower median temperature (37.2 °C) [R19].
Inappropriate hypocapnia in 31 of 34 severe B. rossi dogs [R3].

tests.finding: Low in about 20% of admitted B. rossi dogs [R1].
tests.note: Use an instant method so treatment is not delayed [R9]. Veterinary glucometers read higher than the laboratory, by up to 2 to 3.5 mmol/L; one meter was affected by PCV [R20].

tests.finding: Raised in about half of admitted dogs; repeat at 8 and 16 h [R6][R2].
tests.note: Serial values carry more prognostic weight than one value [R6].

tests.finding: Low potassium and sodium are common; chloride may be high or low [R10][R15].
tests.note: Potassium is often low in icteric dogs [R7]. In B. canis, 3 of 21 non-azotaemic dogs met criteria for inappropriate ADH secretion, linked to low blood pressure [R21].

tests.test: Blood gas with anion gap and albumin
tests.finding: Mixed metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis; negative base excess in all of 34 severe dogs [R3].
tests.note: Median pH was normal (7.43) in 320 dogs, so a normal pH does not exclude a severe disorder [R2].

tests.finding: Cortisol high and T4 low in dogs that die [R4][R2].
tests.note: Research and prognosis only. Do thyroid tests for hypothyroidism after recovery, not in acute illness [R12].

differentials.distinguish: Cerebral babesiosis is defined with a normal or high glucose; correct hypoglycaemia first and reassess (SY07) [R2][R1].
Both can cause collapse and altered mentation with a normal glucose (SY01, SY10) [R9].
Glucose falls in stored blood through glycolysis, more so in inflammatory states; use a fluoride oxalate tube for laboratory samples [R9].
Azotaemia with low sodium and low T3 points to renal involvement (SY05) [R15][R17].

approach.detail: In every admitted dog, and always in collapsed dogs, puppies, and dogs with severe anaemia, vomiting or icterus [R1]. Treat borderline meter values as possibly low [R20].
Diluted 50% dextrose IV, then a dextrose infusion. Recheck glucose hourly until stable [R22][R9].
At admission and again at 8 and 16 h. A lactate that does not halve is a warning sign (SY11 for triage) [R6][R7].
Add potassium chloride to fluids when potassium is low, at no more than 0.5 mmol/kg/h [R23]. Prefer a balanced crystalloid [R24].
Acidosis is driven by hypoxia and hypoperfusion; treat anaemia and perfusion (SY01, SY10). Bicarbonate is not indicated for lactic acidosis [R25][R3].

approach.action: Blood gas and full acid-base analysis
approach.detail: Where available, to detect mixed disorders that pH alone hides [R2][R3].
If glucose will not stay up on dextrose, glucagon infusion has been used in other causes [R26].

treatments.name: Dextrose bolus and infusion
treatments.aim: Correct hypoglycaemia quickly and keep glucose in range.
treatments.evidence_summary: No trial. In the Onderstepoort B. rossi study, 2 hypoglycaemic dogs with seizures recovered fully after IV dextrose, 3 lost their miosis at once, and one collapsed dog responded within 90 seconds of a dextrose bolus [R9]. The authors of B. rossi studies recommend aggressive treatment [R8][R1]. Doses for the infusion come from a general canine review (level D/E) [R22].

doses.context: B. rossi, 1 collapsed dog, case in a dissertation
doses.note: Glucose 2.65 mmol/L; given while a transfusion was started.

doses.route: IV, peripheral vein, slowly over 5 to 10 min
doses.note: Dilute at least 1:2 with saline to reduce phlebitis and haemolysis.

doses.dose: 2.5% to 5% solution, at maintenance fluid rate
doses.note: Adjust the rate to the glucose. Target glucose 3.3 to 8.3 mmol/L, checked hourly.

treatments.cautions: Excess dextrose can cause osmotic diuresis and dehydration; give boluses slowly [R22]. Strong solutions irritate veins [R22].
treatments.monitoring: Glucose hourly until stable on the infusion [R22]. Recurrence after treatment was not reported in babesiosis.

treatments.name: Potassium chloride in intravenous fluids
treatments.evidence_summary: Hypokalaemia is common: 40% of 40 early B. canis dogs [R10], and frequent in 70 B. canis dogs [R15]; in B. rossi it is often low in icteric dogs [R7]. A South African review lists added potassium chloride as part of fluid support [R7]. No study tested supplementation in babesiosis. The rate limit is from a general canine source [R23].

doses.context: General canine and feline medicine, proceedings (level E)
doses.note: This is a maximum rate, not a dose. The source states it in milliequivalents, equal to mmol for potassium. No table of amounts by serum potassium was verified.

treatments.cautions: Faster infusion risks iatrogenic hyperkalaemia and cardiac effects [R23].
treatments.monitoring: Potassium at least daily while on supplemented fluids; no babesiosis source states a schedule.

treatments.name: Early feeding
treatments.aim: Keep glucose up once the dog can eat.
treatments.evidence_summary: A general canine review suggests small frequent meals with complex carbohydrate after the dextrose bolus once mentation is normal [R22]. Hypoglycaemic surviving B. rossi dogs had gone a median 36 hours since their last meal [R19]. Not tested in babesiosis.
treatments.cautions: Only when the dog can swallow safely [R22].
treatments.monitoring: Glucose before and after meals while the infusion is reduced.

treatments.name: Balanced crystalloid as the fluid of choice
treatments.evidence_summary: Severe B. rossi and B. canis babesiosis already has a hyperchloraemic, dilutional acidosis component [R3][R27][R14]. A review of fluid therapy in canine and feline sepsis prefers balanced crystalloids over 0.9% sodium chloride, based mainly on human trials [R24]. No fluid comparison exists in babesiosis. Volumes are on SY10.
treatments.cautions: High-chloride fluids are linked to kidney injury in human sepsis [R24].
treatments.monitoring: Chloride, sodium and acid-base status daily where available.

treatments.name: Glucagon infusion for refractory hypoglycaemia
treatments.evidence_summary: In 9 dogs with hypoglycaemia that did not respond to dextrose, 7 with insulinoma, glucose rose in all on glucagon; 5 survived [R26]. Not used in babesiosis, where insulin is low and liver glycogen may be depleted [R13].

doses.dose: 50 ng/kg bolus, then infusion up to 15 ng/kg/min
doses.note: Both values are medians from the series.

treatments.cautions: Effect may be less if liver glycogen is depleted, as suggested in babesiosis [R13].

treatments.name: Sodium bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis
treatments.evidence_summary: Not studied in babesiosis. Acidaemia marks a high mortality group in B. rossi [R28], but the acidosis is mixed with alkalosis and the median pH is normal [R3][R2]. In human septic shock with lactic acidosis, trials showed no haemodynamic benefit and the guideline suggests against it; it is suggested only for pH 7.2 or less with acute kidney injury [R25].
treatments.cautions: No canine babesiosis dose or indication was found [R25].
treatments.monitoring: Blood gas, sodium and ionised calcium if it is given.

treatments.name: Hydrocortisone or other glucocorticoids for adrenal insufficiency
treatments.aim: Replace cortisol in presumed critical-illness adrenal insufficiency.
treatments.evidence_summary: B. rossi dogs had high basal and ACTH-stimulated cortisol, with no evidence of adrenal insufficiency, and the highest cortisol in dogs that died [R5][R4]. In 47 dogs with septic shock of other causes, survival did not differ with hydrocortisone [R29]. No babesiosis study tested glucocorticoids for this purpose. Steroids for immune-mediated haemolysis are on SY02.
treatments.cautions: No indication shown; cortisol is already high in severe B. rossi disease [R4].

prognosis.text: In 320 B. rossi dogs, 34 (10.6%) died of the disease; the paper does not say whether euthanased dogs are included [R2]. Hypoglycaemia, high and persistent lactate, acidaemia, high cortisol and low thyroxine are all linked with death, but no single marker was an independent predictor [R2][R28].

indicators.meaning: Odds of death 3.47 times higher in B. rossi [R2]; linked with death in 90 dogs [R6].

indicators.finding: Admission lactate above 5 mmol/L, or above 4.1 mmol/L
indicators.meaning: Higher mortality; 4.1 mmol/L gave 75% sensitivity and specificity for death [R7][R2].

indicators.finding: Lactate rising or falling by less than 50% in 8 to 16 h, or persistently above 4.4 mmol/L
indicators.meaning: Strong predictor of death; above 4.4 mmol/L at 24 h predicted death in every case [R6][R7].

indicators.finding: Cortisol above 388 nmol/L or total T4 below 4.8 nmol/L
indicators.meaning: Cut-offs for death in B. rossi (cortisol 87.5% sensitive, 82.9% specific); not validated [R2][R4].
Mortality above 30% in admitted B. rossi dogs, against 12% overall [R28].
Present in all 8 of 8 non-survivors (6 died, 2 euthanased) and 1 of 7 survivors [R16].

related.why: Cerebral babesiosis: hypoglycaemia is its main differential.
Shock and hypotension: fluid volumes and the cause of hyperlactataemia.
Triage and the order of care: lactate and glucose as triage values.
Severe anaemia, which drives hypoglycaemia and lactate.
Acute kidney injury and its electrolyte changes.

evidence_gaps: No study reports how often hypoglycaemia recurs after dextrose in babesiosis, or the best infusion rate.
No study of lactate-guided treatment in babesiosis.
No trial of bicarbonate, potassium or fluid type in babesiosis.
No study tested thyroid hormone in dogs with babesiosis or other non-thyroidal illness; no source supports giving it.
No study tested glucocorticoids for adrenal insufficiency in babesiosis; adrenal insufficiency was not found.
No data on insulin for hyperglycaemia in babesiosis.
Almost no glucose, lactate or endocrine data for B. gibsoni and B. vogeli.

search.note: Local MET synthesis, combined treatment set and article texts; PubMed and Europe PMC for babesiosis with glucose, lactate, acid-base, electrolytes, cortisol and thyroid, and for each candidate treatment. AAHA fluid therapy guidelines (2013, 2024) could not be read (access blocked), so no potassium sliding scale is given. Keller, Nel, Jacobson and Leisewitz 2001 journal papers were read as abstracts only; the Keller dissertation was read in full.
